title: Patterns
summary: Lua patterns as a small alternative to regular expressions, the character classes %d %a %s %w and friends, sets in square brackets, the repeat signs + * - ?, anchors, captures, and string.match.
markdown: ## A small language for text Lua does not have regular expressions. It has **patterns**, which do most of the same work with a much smaller set of rules. `string.match(s, pattern)` returns the first part of `s` that matches, or `nil`: ```lua print(("order 66 shipped"):match("%d+")) print(("hello"):match("%d+")) print(("Version 5.4.7"):match("%d+%.%d+")) ``` ``` 66 nil 5.4 ``` ## Character classes | Class | Matches | Upper case = the opposite | |---|---|---| | `.` | any character | | | `%a` | letters | `%A` not a letter | | `%d` | digits 0-9 | `%D` | | `%l` / `%u` | lower / upper case letters | | | `%s` | whitespace (space, tab, newline) | `%S` | | `%w` | letters and digits | `%W` | | `%p` | punctuation | `%P` | | `%x` | hex digits | | `%` also **escapes** the special characters: `%.` is a real dot, `%%` a real percent sign, `%-` a real minus. (Lua uses `%` where other languages use `\`.) A **set** in square brackets matches one character from it: `[aeiou]` a vowel, `[%w_]` a letter, digit or underscore, `[0-9a-f]` a range. `[^...]` matches any character **not** in the set: `[^,]` anything but a comma. ## Repeats | Sign | Means | |---|---| | `+` | one or more, as many as possible | | `*` | zero or more, as many as possible | | `-` | zero or more, as **few** as possible | | `?` | optional: zero or one | ```lua local s = "bold and it" print(s:match("<.*>")) -- greedy: as much as possible print(s:match("<.->")) -- lazy: as little as possible print(("-42"):match("^-?%d+$"), ("4-2"):match("^-?%d+$")) ``` ``` bold and it -42 nil ``` Repeat signs apply to **one** character class only. Lua patterns cannot repeat a group: there is no `(ab)+`. When you need that, use a loop or a real parser. ## Anchors `^` at the start of a pattern means "only at the start of the text", `$` at the end means "only at the end". With both, the whole text must match, which is how you **validate** input: ```lua local function is_whole_number(s) return s:match("^%d+$") ~= nil end local function is_name(s) return s:match("^[%a_][%w_]*$") ~= nil end print(is_whole_number("123"), is_whole_number("12a"), is_whole_number("")) print(is_name("player_1"), is_name("1player")) ``` ``` true false false true false ``` ## Captures Brackets mark **captures**: the parts you want back. `match` then returns each capture instead of the whole match: ```lua local date = "2026-11-16" local y, m, d = date:match("(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)") print(y, m, d, tonumber(m) + 1) local key, value = (" volume = 11 "):match("^%s*(%w+)%s*=%s*(.-)%s*$") print("[" .. key .. "]", "[" .. value .. "]") print(("John Smith"):match("(%a+) (%a+)")) ``` ``` 2026 11 16 12 [volume] [11] John Smith ``` Captures are always strings: convert numbers with `tonumber`. `%s*(.-)%s*$` is the standard way to capture something with the spaces around it trimmed. Trimming on its own is so common it is worth writing once: ```lua local function trim(s) return (s:match("^%s*(.-)%s*$")) end print("[" .. trim(" padded text ") .. "]") ``` ``` [padded text] ``` `find` works with patterns too and returns the position followed by the captures: ```lua print(("x = 10"):find("(%d+)")) ``` ``` 5 6 10 ``` ## Check yourself ```quiz ? How do you match a literal dot? - `\.` + `%.` - `.` > In Lua patterns `%` escapes a special character; a bare `.` matches any character. `[.]` also works, but `%.` is the usual way, and the backslash of other regex languages does nothing here. ? What is the difference between `.*` and `.-`? - `.*` matches any character and `.-` matches a dash + `.*` takes as much as possible, `.-` as little as possible - `.-` takes as much as possible, `.*` as little as possible > Both repeat any character zero or more times. `.*` is greedy, `.-` is lazy. ? Which pattern checks that the WHOLE string is digits? - "%d+" - "^%d" + "^%d+$" - "[%d]" > ^ and $ anchor the match to the start and end, so nothing else can be around the digits. ? What does `("a1b22c333"):match("%a(%d+)")` give? - "a1" - "333" - 1 + "1" > The first place the pattern matches is "a1", and the capture is the digits: the string "1". ```

cards.q: How do you match a literal dot?
cards.a:
`%.`

In Lua patterns `%` escapes a special character; a bare `.` matches any character. `[.]` also works, but `%.` is the usual way, and the backslash of other regex languages does nothing here.

cards.q: What is the difference between `.*` and `.-`?
cards.a:
`.*` takes as much as possible, `.-` as little as possible

Both repeat any character zero or more times. `.*` is greedy, `.-` is lazy.

cards.q: Which pattern checks that the WHOLE string is digits?
cards.a:
"^%d+$"

^ and $ anchor the match to the start and end, so nothing else can be around the digits.

"1"

The first place the pattern matches is "a1", and the capture is the digits: the string "1".
